newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia stands firm against NATO enlargement plans.
newsitem.headline: Russia stands firm against NATO enlargement plans.

text.p: Russia on Tuesday dismissed suggestions that it was ready to accept NATO's eastward expansion plans as "fantasy" and took a tough line before talks with alliance foreign ministers in Brussels.

"Russia's position on this issue remains firm and rather tough," President Boris Yeltsin's press secretary, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, told a briefing before Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov flew to Brussels to meet NATO foreign ministers.

"It has not changed although our partners in dialogue have tried at various times to send to the world other signals... that Moscow has started to look more flexible, as if it had internally accepted such expansion. No. That is all fantasy."
NATO foreign ministers were meeting in Brussels to fix a date for a summit next year to identify and plan for new members from central and eastern Europe -- former Kremlin Warsaw Pact allies.
Moscow has bitterly opposed the plans, saying they threaten its security.

Primakov, who had agreed his negotiating position with Yeltsin, was due to arrive in Brussels later on Tuesday to meet the alliance foreign ministers and NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana before flying home on Thursday.
Russian officials have been united in fierce opposition to NATO's enlargement plans in recent weeks after several months of wavering between tough rejections and signs of compromise.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin voiced Russia's fears at a summit of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) in Lisbon last week, but most other leaders at the meeting backed NATO's plans.

Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, who is expected to visit Brussels next week, has said one option for responding to NATO enlargement would be to point Russian nuclear missiles at eastern European countries which join the alliance.
"We think there are no arguments supporting NATO's eastward expansion," Yastrzhembsky said.

"It is a step which would lead only to negative consequences, above all for Russia and its national interests, and which to a certain degree would exclude Russia from this part of Europe and isolate Russia."
Despite his harsh comments, Yastrzhembsky said "new ideas" were starting to emerge from Western Europe and that they would be discussed in Brussels.
He gave no details but said: "In Lisbon (at the OSCE summit) we registered a certain change in the tone of the way the Russian arguments were taken."
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said at the start of the NATO foreign ministers' meeting in Brussels that NATO would not station nuclear weapons on the territory of any new member states.
Christopher also said that no NATO nuclear forces were currently on the alert.

His comments were a clear attempt to ease concern in Moscow, which has been seeking such public assurances and appears keen to win as many concessions as possible from NATO before it pushes ahead with expansion.
